name: Tourmaline Pink
lede: Tourmaline Pink is a dusty rose first plated by Ridgway in 1912, close enough to [[puce]] on screen that the two are nearly interchangeable to the eye.

sections.title: A dusty rose, rarely used
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 color atlas plates this rose at plate XXXVIII, hue 67 double-prime, tone b, a scan of an aged plate that our sources treat as approximate [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS circular later classed it as grayish purplish red, within 1.0 unit of its block center, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary cites the same 1912 record rather than adding a new one [1]. The Munsell notation is 5.8RP 6.0/6.7 [1]. Our sources say nothing about why the name pairs "tourmaline" with pink; the gemstone itself runs from pink to green to black, and the color-word classification here only files Tourmaline Pink as a mineral name, with no documented coiner [1].

The closest named color on screen is [[puce]], 3.2 units away and described as almost the same; [[cosmos]] and [[bright-mauve]] follow at 3.4 and 3.9, both read as purpler; [[dusky-pink]] sits at 4.1, redder and more vivid [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is a rare color in our painting archive: it appears in only 0.06 percent of 23,781 paintings, 15 of them, and the within-painting lens isolates it as a dominant area in just 4, as photographed [2]. That ranks it rarer than 77 percent of the named colors we track [2]. The earliest match is a painting dated to 1560, 352 years before Ridgway's 1912 record of the name; that gap marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not the pigment itself, and with only 7 dated matches in total the pattern is thin, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

origin.source: Ridgway, Color Standards and Color Nomenclature
